name: Stanford HAI AI Index: Annual Macro Data on AI and Nonprofits
title: Stanford HAI AI Index: Annual Macro Data on AI and Nonprofits
answer: Stanford HAI's AI Index is an annual report series tracking AI's technical progress, investment, adoption, policy and social impact, published by Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered AI. For readers following AI in nonprofits, its most useful contribution is longitudinal, cross-sector evidence: organizational adoption reached 88% in the 2026 edition, up from 78% in 2024 and 55% in 2023, alongside documented incidents, regulation counts and public opinion data that mission-driven organizations can cite.

sections.body: The AI Index is published by Stanford HAI, Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. It is an annual report series, with editions reviewed here from 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, plus chapter pages such as the Economy chapters of the 2024 and 2026 reports. Each report landing page presents the edition's mission and a list of key findings, and the chapters break out topics including economy, technical performance, policy, public opinion and education. The series is a reference work rather than a membership or events site, and it is dated by edition year.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Across editions the AI Index documents a shift in AI production and adoption from academia to industry. The 2023 report notes that until 2014 most significant machine learning models came from academia, but in 2022 there were 32 significant industry-produced models against three from academia. The 2024 report puts 2023 at 51 notable industry models, 15 from academia and 21 from collaborations. The 2026 report says industry produced over 90% of notable frontier models in 2025. Adoption figures climb in parallel: 55% of organizations used AI in 2023, 78% in 2024 and 88% in the 2026 edition. Investment data show the United States far ahead of China, at $285.9 billion against $12.4 billion in 2025, and generative AI attracting $33.9 billion globally in 2024. The reports also track harms and governance: documented AI incidents rose to 362 in the 2026 edition from 233 in 2024, and U.S. AI-related regulations grew from one in 2016 to 25 in 2023. Public opinion data show concern rising, with 52% of Americans more concerned than excited in 2024, up from 38% in 2022.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The 2026 report states organizational adoption reached 88%, that 4 in 5 university students use generative AI, that U.S. private AI investment reached $285.9 billion in 2025, that documented AI incidents rose to 362 from 233 in 2024, and that generative AI reached 53% population adoption within three years. The 2025 report states 78% of organizations reported using AI in 2024, up from 55% the year before, and that the FDA approved 223 AI-enabled medical devices in 2023, up from six in 2015. The 2024 report states generative AI funding nearly octupled from 2022 to $25.2 billion, and that 52% of Americans reported feeling more concerned than excited about AI, rising from 38% in 2022. The 2023 report states global AI private investment was $91.9 billion in 2022, and that AI incidents and controversies increased 26 times since 2012.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: Nonprofits operate in the same adoption and funding environment the AI Index measures, and the series supplies the macro numbers that grant proposals, board papers and programme design often need. The organizational adoption trend, from 55% to 78% to 88% across three editions, gives a defensible baseline for arguing that AI use is now mainstream rather than experimental. The incident counts and regulation counts give risk and governance context for organizations weighing duty-of-care and compliance questions. The public opinion data, showing rising nervousness toward AI, are directly relevant to how nonprofits communicate about AI-enabled services to the communities they serve. The education and workforce findings, including student AI use and AI-related job postings, inform workforce and digital inclusion programmes.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: The AI Index is a macro measurement series, not a nonprofit sector study. Its adoption figures cover organizations generally, and the pages reviewed do not break out nonprofit, charitable or civil society organizations as a category. The reports are dated by edition, so figures age quickly in a fast-moving field, and several findings rest on third-party surveys such as McKinsey, Ipsos and Pew rather than the Index's own primary collection. The chapter pages reviewed cover economy and selected topics only, and the series does not offer operational guidance, tool recommendations or programme-level case studies for nonprofits.
